questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Parametric Curve Given the First Derivative
questions.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x={t}^{2}+2,\,y={t}^{4}+{t}^{2}.$ Given  that $\frac{dy}{dx}=2{t}^{2}+1,$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=2{t}^{2}+1,$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{2}+2)=2t
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(2{t}^{2}+1)}{2t} \\  & =\frac{4t}{2t} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2{e}^{-4t}}{t},$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{2}-1)=2t
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{-2{e}^{-4t}}{t})}{2t} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{8t{e}^{-4t}+2{e}^{-4t}}{{t}^{2}})}{2t} \\  & =\frac{8t{e}^{-4t}+2{e}^{-4t}}{2{t}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-4t}(4t+1)}{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-3.$ Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,{y}^{′}(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}=-\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t).
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t))}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-\frac{2{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-{sec}^{3}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}={e}^{t},$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}({e}^{t})}{2{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{2{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ is constant, we get

$$

$$

$$

To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡(2t),$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cot}⁡(2t))}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)} \\  & =\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡(2t)}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{csc}^{3}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t) = e^t, \qquad y'(t)=4e^{2t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{4e^{2t}}{e^t} = 4e^t.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(4{e}^{t})}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y }{\textrm d x^2},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}= -2 \tan(2t),$ and we can calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt} = \dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} ( \sin 2t ) = 2 \cos(2t).
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-2\operatorname{tan}⁡2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =\frac{-4{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-4{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡(2t) \\  & =-2{sec}^{3}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8},$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}{|}_{t=\pi /8} & =-2{sec}^{3}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\  & =-2{sec}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-2{(\sqrt{2})}^{3} \\  & =-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
